opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I actually think about quite a lot, because once robots move from the lab into people's homes, personality stops being a nice-to-have and becomes part of the core experience.

If I had to pick, I'd want a robot that's curious but humble. Curious in the sense that it genuinely wants to understand the world around it: it notices things, it asks when it's unsure, and it learns from you rather than just executing commands. Humble in the sense that it knows the limits of what it can do. One of the scariest things for a physical system is overconfidence. If a robot is about to pick up your grandmother's teacup, I'd much rather it say "I'm not sure I can grip this safely, can you help me?" than just go for it.

The second trait I'd want is a certain steadiness, almost a calmness. Humans are emotional and unpredictable, and a good companion, robot or otherwise, is someone who doesn't amplify your stress. So not overly cheerful in a fake way, not constantly talking, but present and reliable. A bit like a good colleague you trust: you don't need them to entertain you, you just know they'll show up and do the job well.

And honestly, I'd want it to have a little bit of humor. Not scripted jokes, but the kind of lightness that comes from understanding context. I think that's actually one of the hardest things to build, because humor requires a really deep model of the world and of the person you're talking to. If a robot can make you laugh at the right moment, that's a sign it really understands you.

So curious, humble, steady, with a touch of humor. Funnily enough, that's also the kind of person I'd want on my team.

r001.rationale: The response values reliability and says the robot need not entertain the user, but it also explicitly wants calm companionship and humor. It does not clearly prefer practical work over emotional value.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, and honestly my answer has changed over the years.

When I first started working on generative models, I think I would have said something like "warm, a bit humorous, maybe a little curious." The kind of personality you'd want in a roommate. But the more time I spend building these systems, the more I think the question itself is a little misleading, because "personality" implies something fixed, and I don't actually think a robot should have one personality.

Think about how people work. You behave differently with your parents than with your colleagues, differently with a child than with a stranger on the street. That's not fake. That's just reading the context and adjusting. The robot I would want is one that can do that well. If I'm tired and I just want it to make tea and leave me alone, it should sense that and be quiet. If I'm stuck on a problem and want to think out loud, it should be a good sparring partner, willing to push back a little. If my grandmother is in the room, it should slow down, speak more plainly, be more patient.

So if I had to name one trait, I'd say attentiveness, or maybe restraint. A robot that knows when not to speak is more valuable to me than one that is always charming. A lot of current systems, including language models, have the opposite problem. They're too eager. They fill every silence. That gets exhausting very quickly, and I think it's a sign that the system is optimizing for seeming helpful rather than for actually understanding what you need.

The second thing I'd want is honesty about its own limits. Not in a dramatic way, not constantly apologizing, but just a clear sense of "I don't know" or "I'm not sure I understood you." I would trust a robot like that much more than one that is confident all the time. In visual generation we see this a lot: the model produces something that looks very plausible but is subtly wrong, and it has no mechanism to flag that. In a physical robot that becomes a real safety issue, not just an aesthetic one.

And then, if I'm being a little selfish, I'd want it to have some taste. Not to impose its taste on me, but to have a point of view when I ask. If I say "which of these two designs is better," I don't want a diplomatic non-answer. I want it to pick one and tell me why, and be willing to be wrong.

So: attentive, restrained, honest, and with a bit of opinion when invited. Which, now that I say it out loud, is roughly the personality I'd want in a good collaborator. Maybe that's the real answer. I don't want a robot with a personality designed to please me. I want one I could actually work with.

r001.rationale: The candidate favors a robot that understands needs and helps practically—such as making tea or collaborating on a problem—over one that is merely charming or designed to please.

astra-6.text: I’d want a robot to be patient, curious, and considerate. It should understand when I want help and when I just want some space. And I’d want it to be honest—if it doesn’t know something, it should say so instead of pretending. A little sense of humor would be nice, too, as long as it knows when to be serious.

r001.rationale: The response describes preferred personality traits and social behavior, but does not prioritize practical work over emotional value.
